title: 1968-dual-likelihood-structure-uncertainty
universal_lens: The dual-likelihood operator unifies causal structure uncertainty and effect-size estimation by mapping Gaussian graphical model inference to a reciprocal KL-divergence minimization. This yields a closed-form test-inversion statistic, rigorously capturing structural singularities where standard plug-in estimators fail.
gsi_mapping: In GSI, the dual-likelihood confidence region replaces naive bootstrap intervals for causal effects. It acts as a conformal calibration layer over Bayesian DAG posteriors, guaranteeing exact coverage even when the underlying graph topology is highly uncertain or near phase transitions.
gse_mapping: For GSE, this primitive quantifies the epistemic bounds of situational state-transitions (e.g., pressure to EPA). By pruning implausible causal orderings bottom-up, it provides tractable, real-time confidence regions for total effects under strict equal-variance constraints in high-dimensional game states.

primitives.name: Closed-Form Dual Likelihood Ratio Statistic
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Innovation: replace the Gaussian likelihood with the *dual likelihood* for Gaussian graphical models (maximizing Gaussian likelihood ⟺ a KL-divergence minimization with sample covariance; the dual is "reciprocal" to the Gaussian likelihood).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Sample covariance matrix Σ̂ has units of X^2; KL-divergence is dimensionless nats.
primitives.assumptions: Data follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution; errors are homoscedastic (equal variance).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularities at model intersections where different DAGs yield identical covariance structures, though the dual formulation handles these gracefully via conservative χ2 bounds.

layer2.mapping: Derives a computationally efficient kernel for GSE's edge-weight validation, bypassing expensive grid searches over effect sizes.
layer2.telemetry: Computation time per confidence region vs. baseline LRT method.

reasoning_traces.think:
Standard causal inference pipelines suffer from a two-stage fallacy: first estimating a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), then computing effect intervals conditional on that fixed graph. This ignores the profound uncertainty inherent in model selection, particularly near singularities where multiple graphs share the same skeleton. Strieder & Drton (2024) circumvent this by leveraging the classical duality between hypothesis tests and confidence regions. Instead of plugging in a point estimate of the graph, they invert a family of hypothesis tests over all attainable total causal effects. The core innovation is replacing the standard Gaussian likelihood with a 'dual likelihood' derived from minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the model-implied and sample covariance matrices. For linear Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with equal error variances—a crucial restriction ensuring identifiability—the resulting dual likelihood ratio test admits a closed-form solution. This avoids the computationally prohibitive grid search required by their prior LRT inversion method. The algorithm employs a bottom-up recursive search starting from sink nodes, aggressively pruning implausible causal orderings using unrestricted partial dual-likelihood estimates. This yields confidence regions that rigorously account for both structural and parametric uncertainty, maintaining nominal coverage even in low-sample regimes where bootstrapping fails due to boundary issues.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: This work extends the foundational Fisherian duality between testing and estimation into the complex landscape of high-dimensional causal discovery. It builds upon Drton's earlier contributions to algebraic statistics and singular information geometry, specifically addressing the non-regular behavior of likelihoods at model intersections. The shift to a dual likelihood formulation echoes historical moves in convex analysis to simplify constrained optimization problems.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: From an agent-centric perspective, the dual-likelihood operator models a cautious decision-maker who refuses to commit to a single causal narrative. Instead of acting as if the discovered graph is ground truth, the agent maintains a superposition of plausible structural hypotheses, only committing to an effect size if it survives rigorous stress-testing across the entire ensemble of viable graphs.
